author: Arethas of Caesarea
occasion: Three epigrams (two verse, one prose) commemorating deceased women, Anna and Febronia, preserved as fragments in a manuscript of commentary on the Epistle to the Romans.
argument: The first epigram is a first-person lament spoken by Anna herself (or a persona), who died at twenty-three, leaving her aged parents and noble brothers to mourn her; she was widowed and childless, never seeing a child playing at her breast. The second epigram praises Anna's character, her obedience to parents, her noble lineage, and her shining distinction as a woman married to one husband, arguing that her grave cannot obscure these because her life was a lesson and the inscription will speak if all else is silent. The third epigram praises Febronia for her compassion to the poor and her consecration as a bride of Christ, and suggests that even the dead remember her beneficence.

outline.move: A first-person lament spoken by Anna (or a persona), who died at twenty-three after being widowed and childless, leaving her aged parents tearing their white hair and a chorus of noble brothers groaning to mourn her.

A prose epigram arguing that Anna's grave cannot obscure her character, obedience to parents, noble birth, and her shining distinction as a woman married to one husband, because her life was a lesson and the inscription will speak.
